clinicalPearls: Presents as a painful, hot, tender, often fluctuant breast lump with overlying erythema and systemic features such as fever and malaise
Lactational abscesses typically follow mastitis with milk stasis and are most often due to Staphylococcus aureus, frequently entering through a cracked nipple
Non-lactational abscesses are strongly associated with smoking and periductal mastitis and tend to occur near the areola, often with mixed and anaerobic organisms
Established abscesses are best managed by ultrasound-guided needle aspiration, repeated if necessary, with incision and drainage reserved for large, multiloculated, or overlying-necrosis cases
Appropriate antibiotics active against the likely organisms are given alongside drainage; antibiotics alone rarely cure a collection
Breastfeeding or expression from the affected side should generally continue to relieve stasis in lactational cases
A non-lactational or non-resolving abscess, particularly in an older woman, requires exclusion of inflammatory breast cancer and other malignancy
Recurrent periareolar abscess with a mammary duct fistula may need duct excision once inflammation settles
reference.pathophysiology: A breast abscess is a localised collection of pus within breast tissue. In lactating women, milk stasis and nipple trauma allow skin organisms, chiefly Staphylococcus aureus, to enter and proliferate, progressing from mastitis to a walled-off abscess. In non-lactating women, periductal mastitis, strongly linked to smoking, causes duct damage, squamous metaplasia, and duct obstruction, with secondary infection by mixed aerobic and anaerobic organisms producing periareolar collections and sometimes a mammary duct fistula. Untreated collections enlarge, may point to the skin, and can cause tissue necrosis.
additionalDifferentials: Hidradenitis of the inframammary or axillary skin
additionalInvestigations: Breast ultrasound to confirm a collection and guide aspiration
Culture and sensitivity of aspirated pus or milk to direct antibiotic choice
Mammography and core biopsy where malignancy must be excluded, especially non-lactational or non-resolving cases
Assessment of smoking status and diabetes in recurrent non-lactational disease
redFlags: Non-resolving or recurrent inflammatory changes suggesting inflammatory breast cancer
Overlying skin necrosis or spreading cellulitis with systemic sepsis
Immunosuppression or diabetes with rapidly progressive infection
A persistent mass after treatment requiring triple assessment
reference.prognosis: Most breast abscesses resolve fully with timely drainage and appropriate antibiotics. Non-lactational and smoking-related disease is prone to recurrence and mammary duct fistula, and outcome improves with smoking cessation and, when indicated, duct excision.
pitfalls: Treating with antibiotics alone and failing to drain an established collection
Missing inflammatory breast cancer masquerading as a non-resolving abscess
Advising cessation of breastfeeding unnecessarily, worsening milk stasis
Not addressing smoking in recurrent non-lactational disease
references: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
management: Drain the collection by ultrasound-guided needle aspiration, repeated as required, reserving incision and drainage for large, multiloculated, or overlying-necrosis cases

Give antibiotics active against the likely organisms alongside drainage, with anti-staphylococcal cover such as flucloxacillin for lactational disease and added anaerobic cover such as co-amoxiclav or metronidazole for periareolar non-lactational disease
Send aspirated pus or milk for culture and sensitivity to direct antibiotic choice
Continue breastfeeding or expression from the affected side in lactational cases to relieve milk stasis, with analgesia and warm compresses for symptom relief
Support smoking cessation in non-lactational periductal disease to reduce recurrence
Exclude malignancy with mammography and core biopsy in non-resolving or non-lactational cases
Consider duct excision for recurrent periductal disease or an established mammary duct fistula, and refer to a breast surgical service
